meta.title: Neck Pain: Ergonomics and Gentle Strengthening
meta.summary: How to set up your desk, phone, car and pillow — and a short daily programme of gentle neck and shoulder-blade exercises that has good evidence behind it.

paras: Your head weighs about five kilograms and sits on top of a narrow, mobile column of seven small joints, held up by muscles that are working every minute you are awake. Neck pain is common for the same reason shoulder ache is common in someone carrying a bag all day: not because anything is broken, but because a modest load applied for a long time is hard work.

That is the good news. It means the two levers that matter are **how the load is arranged** — your desk, your phone, your car, your pillow — and **how much endurance the supporting muscles have**. Both are things you can change, and neither requires a gym.

box.title: An honest word about posture
box.text: You have probably been told that bad posture causes neck pain. The evidence for that is weaker than the confidence with which it is asserted: studies find only a modest and inconsistent relationship between how people hold their heads and whether their necks hurt. What matters more is **how long you stay in one position** and how much muscular endurance you have. So the advice here is not 'sit up straight' — it is 'move often, and build endurance'.

blocks.title: Why necks ache
blocks.lede: Four contributors, in roughly the order they matter.

cards.title: Duration, not position
body: Any position becomes uncomfortable if you hold it for three hours. Static muscle work restricts its own blood supply, and the ache that follows is the result. Breaking the time up matters more than perfecting the position.

cards.title: Poor endurance in the deep muscles
body: Small deep muscles at the front of the neck are meant to hold the head steady all day. When they fatigue, the big surface muscles take over — and they are sprinters, not marathon runners. They tire, tighten and ache.

cards.title: Your eyes drag your head forwards
body: Screens that are too low, too far away, or too small pull the head forwards without you noticing. A great deal of 'neck strain' is really a vision problem — including out-of-date glasses and the reading segment of multifocals.

cards.title: Stress and jaw clenching
body: Neck and jaw muscles are among the first to tighten under stress, and clenching at night is very common. If your neck pain tracks your stress levels, treat the stress as part of the neck treatment — my [stress management page]({{links.stress}}) covers the techniques.

blocks.title: Setting up the workstation
blocks.lede: Spend twenty minutes doing this properly once. It outperforms almost anything else on this page.

blocks.caption: Sit-stand desks are useful mainly because they make you change position — the benefit comes from the changing, not from the standing. If you have one, alternate every 30 to 60 minutes rather than standing all day.

blocks.title: The rule that beats all of the above
blocks.text: **Get up every 30 to 45 minutes.** No workstation setup survives three unbroken hours. Set a timer, or hook it to something natural — the end of each meeting, each phone call, each chapter. And every 20 minutes, look at something at least six metres away for 20 seconds; it rests the eye muscles that are quietly pulling your head forwards.

blocks.title: The daily programme
blocks.subtitle: About ten minutes. Expect the first improvement at four to six weeks, and the real gains by three months.

items.title: Your phone
paras: Bring the phone up towards your face rather than dropping your head towards the phone. Rest your elbows on a table, a cushion or your other hand, so your arms are not holding the weight.

Be sceptical of the 'text neck' headlines: looking down does increase the load on the neck, but the claim that phones are causing an epidemic of neck damage runs well ahead of the evidence. Duration is again the real issue — a long session in any position is the problem, not the position itself.

items.title: Your pillow
paras: There is no single best pillow, and expensive ones have not been shown to outperform cheap ones. What matters is that your head is supported in line with your body: on your side, the pillow must fill the gap between your ear and the mattress; on your back, it should support the hollow of your neck without pushing your head forwards.
Do not sleep on your front. It requires you to turn your head to one end of its range for hours at a time, and it is the commonest cause of waking with a locked, painful neck.
A rolled towel inside the pillowcase, positioned under the neck, is a cheap and often very effective experiment before you buy anything.

items.title: Driving
paras: Sit tall with the seat upright enough that your shoulders touch the backrest. Set the head restraint so its middle is level with the top of your ears and as close to the back of your head as is comfortable — this is a genuine protection against whiplash in a rear-end collision, not a headrest for comfort.
On long drives, stop every couple of hours and do the two-minute desk reset.

items.title: Carrying things
paras: A heavy bag on one shoulder for years is a real and reversible cause of one-sided neck ache. Use a backpack with both straps, or swap sides deliberately and often, or use a wheeled case.

items.title: Heat, and what to do in a flare
paras: Heat for 15 to 20 minutes helps most people with muscular neck pain, and is worth doing before the exercises rather than instead of them. Ice suits some people better after an acute strain — use whichever works for you.
Keep moving the neck gently through a flare. Rest and collars prolong recovery; that has been shown repeatedly, including after whiplash injuries.

a: Almost never. Collars weaken the muscles you need and slow recovery, including after whiplash, where early gentle movement produces better outcomes than immobilisation. There are specific exceptions after fractures or surgery, which will be explained to you at the time.

items.q: "Is it safe to crack my own neck?"
a: The habit of forcefully twisting your own neck to make it click is worth breaking: it gives brief relief through joint receptors, does nothing lasting, and tends to become compulsive. I would also avoid vigorous high-velocity manipulation of the neck by others — the risk of arterial injury is very small but it is not zero, and gentler treatments work about as well.

items.q: "My scan shows degenerative changes and disc bulges."
a: So does almost everyone's after middle age, including people with no pain whatsoever. These findings correlate poorly with symptoms. They matter when they line up with a specific pattern of arm pain, weakness or numbness — which is precisely what your examination is for.

items.q: "The pain goes down my arm with pins and needles."
a: That suggests irritation of a nerve root, which behaves differently from muscular neck pain. Most cases improve over weeks to a few months. Tell me about it — particularly if there is weakness, if the arm pain is worse than the neck pain, or if it is not settling — and be cautious with end-range neck movements in the meantime.

items.q: "How hard should I push these exercises?"
a: Gently. The chin nod is nearly invisible from the outside, and the isometrics use a third of your strength. Neck exercises that hurt more afterwards were done too hard. Progress by adding time and repetitions before adding effort.

Four to six weeks for the first clear change, and around three months for the substantial gains — that is the timeframe in the trials of neck strengthening, some of which followed people for a year with benefits sustained. The exercises need to become a permanent, small part of your week rather than a course you finish.

blocks.title: Contact me, or seek urgent care, if you have
list: **Weakness, clumsiness or numbness in the hands**, difficulty with buttons or handwriting, or unsteadiness in walking — these can indicate pressure on the spinal cord and need prompt assessment.
**Any change in bladder or bowel control** alongside neck symptoms — this needs emergency assessment.
Neck pain after significant trauma or a car accident.
Neck pain with **fever, unexplained weight loss, or a history of cancer**.
A sudden, severe, unfamiliar neck pain or headache, particularly with dizziness, double vision, slurred speech or facial numbness — this needs emergency assessment.
Progressive arm weakness, or arm pain that is worsening rather than settling.
Neck pain with severe headache and neck stiffness on bending the chin to the chest, with fever or feeling unwell.
Rheumatoid arthritis or Down syndrome with new neck pain — the upper neck joints require specific care in both.
